purpose: Ondansetron is used to prevent and treat nausea and vomiting. It is commonly used after surgery, chemotherapy, or radiation therapy. Sometimes doctors prescribe it for stomach illnesses or morning sickness during pregnancy.
how_it_works: Your body releases a chemical called serotonin when your stomach or gut gets irritated, and that chemical sends a signal to your brain telling it to make you feel sick. Ondansetron blocks the spots in your gut and brain where that serotonin signal would normally attach. By blocking those spots, it stops the nausea and vomiting signal from getting through.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include headache, constipation, feeling tired or drowsy, and dizziness. Some people notice a warm or flushed feeling. These are usually mild and go away on their own.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have a heart condition or an irregular heartbeat, because ondansetron can sometimes affect your heart rhythm, especially at higher doses. Let your doctor know if you take other medications, as some drugs can interact with it and increase this heart risk. Avoid it if you are allergic to ondansetron or similar medicines. If you have liver problems, your doctor may need to lower your dose. Rarely, it can cause a serious reaction called serotonin syndrome if combined with certain other medications — signs include agitation, confusion, fast heart rate, or muscle twitching.
typical_dosing: For nausea and vomiting in adults, a common dose is 4 mg to 8 mg taken by mouth. It can be taken as a regular tablet, a dissolvable tablet that melts on your tongue, or as a liquid. It is often taken about 30 minutes before chemotherapy or surgery, then repeated every 4 to 8 hours as needed. Your doctor will give you the exact schedule that is right for your situation.
